whatIs: The UUID Generator creates universally unique identifiers in two formats: UUID v4 (a 128-bit random number displayed as 32 hexadecimal characters with hyphens in the standard 8-4-4-4-12 layout) and ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier, a 128-bit value that encodes the current timestamp in the first 10 characters followed by 26 random characters in Crockford's Base32 alphabet). Both formats produce identifiers that are practically guaranteed to be unique across all devices and all time, without requiring coordination between systems.
howToUse: Select the identifier format from the dropdown — UUID v4 for standard random identifiers, ULID for time-sortable identifiers.
Set the count — generate between 1 and 1000 identifiers at once. ULIDs are particularly useful for database primary keys because they sort chronologically.
Choose the case — lowercase (default) or UPPERCASE. Some systems require uppercase UUIDs in HTTP headers.
Click Generate to produce the identifiers. Each run produces cryptographically random values using the Web Crypto API's crypto.getRandomValues().
Copy the output — each identifier is on its own line. For single identifiers, use the copy button; for batches, the entire list is copied at once.
whyUse: UUIDs and ULIDs solve the distributed systems problem of generating unique identifiers without a central authority. When multiple servers, microservices, or offline clients need to create records independently, they can each generate UUIDs locally with zero coordination and be confident the IDs will never collide. UUID v4 is the most common format — it's what most databases, APIs, and message queues expect. ULIDs add a time-sorting advantage: they lexicographically sort in creation order, making them ideal for database primary keys where insertion order matters. The ULID timestamp portion uses millisecond precision, so you can extract the creation time from the identifier itself.

faq.q: What's the difference between UUID v4 and ULID?
faq.a: UUID v4 is 128 bits of pure randomness (version 4 indicates random generation). ULID splits the 128 bits into a 48-bit millisecond timestamp and 80 bits of randomness. ULIDs sort chronologically when sorted as strings; UUIDs do not. UUID v4 is the industry standard (RFC 4122); ULID is newer and preferred for database keys where insertion order matters.

faq.q: Can two UUID v4 values ever collide?
faq.a: The probability of collision for UUID v4 is approximately 2^-122 (about 1 in 5.3 × 10^36). This is so small that you could generate 1 billion UUIDs per second for 85 years and still have only a 50% chance of a single collision. For practical purposes, UUID v4 collisions never happen.

faq.q: Why use ULID instead of auto-incrementing integers?
faq.a: Auto-incrementing integers require a central counter, which becomes a bottleneck in distributed systems. ULIDs can be generated independently by any node without coordination. They also encode creation time (extractable from the first 10 characters), which is useful for debugging and audit logs. The tradeoff is larger storage (16 bytes vs 4-8 bytes for an integer) and less human-readable values.

faq.q: Is this compatible with databases?
faq.a: Yes. UUID v4 works as a primary key in PostgreSQL (uuid type), MySQL (CHAR(36) or BINARY(16)), MongoDB (stored natively), and most ORMs. ULIDs can be stored as strings or converted to 128-bit integers. Some databases have native ULID support or extensions.

whatIs: The Htpasswd Generator creates Apache htpasswd-format credential entries by hashing a password with bcrypt and formatting the output as username:hash — the standard format used by Apache, Nginx, and other web servers for HTTP Basic Authentication. The tool uses the bcryptjs library to produce a salted bcrypt hash with configurable cost rounds, producing output that can be directly added to an htpasswd file.
howToUse: Enter a username in the Username field — this becomes the identifier in the htpasswd entry (default: admin).
Enter the password in the input panel — this is the plaintext password that will be hashed.
Set the bcrypt rounds (cost factor) — the default is 10, which provides a good balance between security and performance. Higher rounds increase security but slow down hashing.
Read the output — the result is in username:hash format, for example: admin:$2a$10$xK7... The hash starts with $2a$10$ indicating bcrypt with 10 rounds.
Add the output line to your htpasswd file — each line in the file is one username:hash pair.
whyUse: HTTP Basic Authentication is the simplest way to password-protect a web page, staging server, or API endpoint. The htpasswd file format is the standard way to store these credentials — it's supported by Apache's AuthBasicProvider, Nginx's htpasswd module, and CI/CD tools like GitHub Actions. The tool produces bcrypt hashes, which are the recommended algorithm for htpasswd files (as opposed to the older MD5 or crypt formats) because bcrypt includes a salt and a configurable cost factor that makes brute-force attacks prohibitively expensive.

faq.q: What bcrypt rounds should I use?
faq.a: The default of 10 rounds is appropriate for most use cases. Each increase in rounds doubles the computation time — 11 rounds takes twice as long as 10, 12 rounds takes four times as long. For high-security applications, 12-14 rounds are reasonable. For development/staging servers where login speed matters, 10 is fine. The hash output always starts with $2a$N$ where N is the rounds value.

faq.q: Can I use this with Nginx?
faq.a: Yes. Nginx supports htpasswd files via the auth_basic and auth_basic_user_file directives. Install the htpasswd utility (apache2-utils on Debian/Ubuntu) or use this tool to generate entries, then add them to your htpasswd file. Nginx reads bcrypt hashes natively.

faq.q: Is this secure for production?
faq.a: For simple password protection of staging servers, admin panels, or internal tools — yes. For user authentication in a production web application, use a proper authentication framework (Passport.js, NextAuth, etc.) with session management, rate limiting, and account lockout. HTTP Basic Auth has no built-in protection against brute-force attacks beyond what your server provides.

faq.q: How do I create a new htpasswd file?
faq.a: Each line in an htpasswd file is a username:hash pair. Create a new file, paste the output from this tool, and add more lines for additional users. The file has no header or footer — just one entry per line. Protect the file with appropriate filesystem permissions (chmod 640 or similar).

whatIs: The JWT Validator takes a JSON Web Token and checks whether it is structurally valid — verifying that it has exactly three dot-separated segments, that each segment is valid Base64URL encoding, that the header specifies a known algorithm, and that the payload contains standard JWT claims (exp, iat, nbf). It also calculates the token's entropy, checks for common misconfigurations, and reports whether the token appears to be expired based on the exp claim.
howToUse: Paste a complete JWT (the three dot-separated Base64URL segments) into the input panel.
Read the validation output — the tool checks structural validity, algorithm, expiration, and claim presence.
Check the expiration status — if the exp claim exists, the tool reports whether the token has expired or when it will expire.
Review the warnings — the tool flags common issues like missing exp, weak algorithms (none, HS256 with short secrets), and suspicious claim values.
whyUse: JWT tokens are ubiquitous in modern authentication, but they're easy to get wrong. Common mistakes include using the 'none' algorithm (which means unsigned tokens), missing expiration claims (which means tokens are valid forever), and using weak HMAC secrets. This validator catches these issues before you deploy a token to production. It also helps debug token-related errors: when an API rejects a token, pasting it here quickly reveals whether the token is structurally valid or has an obvious problem.

faq.q: What does 'algorithm: none' mean?
faq.a: The 'none' algorithm means the token is not cryptographically signed — anyone can create or modify it. This is a critical security vulnerability. If your JWT library accepts 'none' algorithm tokens, an attacker can forge arbitrary claims (like admin permissions) without knowing any secret. Always reject tokens with algorithm 'none'.

faq.q: Does this verify the signature?
faq.a: No — this tool validates structure, claims, and configuration. Signature verification requires the signing key (HMAC secret or RSA/ECDSA public key), which this client-side tool doesn't have. Use the JWT RS256 Verifier tool for signature verification with a public key, or the JWT HS256 Verifier for HMAC verification with a shared secret.

faq.q: What are the standard JWT claims?
faq.a: Standard claims include: exp (expiration time), iat (issued at), nbf (not before), sub (subject/user ID), iss (issuer), aud (audience), and jti (JWT ID). Not all claims are required, but exp is strongly recommended — a token without expiration is valid forever if stolen.

faq.q: How do I fix an expired token?
faq.a: Expired tokens cannot be 'fixed' — they must be reissued. Your authentication flow should include a refresh token mechanism: when the access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to the auth server to get a new access token. If you don't have refresh tokens, the user must log in again.

whatIs: The JWT HS256 Verifier verifies that a JSON Web Token signed with the HMAC-SHA256 algorithm is authentic by recomputing the signature using a shared secret you provide. Paste the JWT and the secret key, and the tool decodes the token, recomputes the HMAC signature, and compares it to the token's signature — if they match, the token is verified as authentic and unmodified.
howToUse: Paste the complete JWT into the input panel — all three dot-separated segments.
Enter the HMAC secret key in the Secret field — this is the same secret used to sign the token.
Click Verify — the tool recomputes the HMAC-SHA256 signature and compares it to the token's signature.
Read the result — Valid means the signature matches and the token is authentic. Invalid means the signature doesn't match, the token was modified, or the wrong secret was used.
Check the payload — the decoded payload shows all claims, including expiration status.
whyUse: HS256 is the most common JWT signing algorithm — it's used by Auth0, AWS Cognito, and many OAuth2 providers. It uses a shared secret (both the signer and verifier know the same key), which makes it simpler than RSA-based algorithms but requires secure secret management. This tool lets you verify tokens without running a server or installing a JWT library — useful for debugging authentication flows, testing token generation, and understanding how HMAC verification works.

faq.q: What is the difference between HS256 and RS256?
faq.a: HS256 uses a shared secret (symmetric) — both the signer and verifier use the same key. RS256 uses a key pair (asymmetric) — the signer uses a private key, and anyone can verify with the public key. RS256 is more secure for distributed systems because the verification key can be public. HS256 is simpler and faster, but the secret must be shared securely with all verifiers.

faq.q: My secret is a Base64 string — do I decode it first?
faq.a: It depends on how the token was signed. If the signing library used the raw bytes of the Base64 string (without decoding), use the Base64 string as-is. If it decoded the Base64 first, you need to decode it before pasting. Check your token generation code to see which approach was used. Most libraries use the raw string, not the decoded bytes.

faq.q: Can I verify any JWT algorithm with this tool?
faq.a: No — this tool specifically verifies HS256 (HMAC-SHA256). For RS256, ES256, or other asymmetric algorithms, use the JWT RS256 Verifier tool. The algorithm is specified in the token's header — check the alg field to know which verification tool to use.

faq.q: What happens if I use the wrong secret?
faq.a: The tool will report the token as Invalid. The HMAC signature is computed from the payload and the secret — a different secret produces a completely different signature. This is by design: only someone with the correct secret can verify the token. The tool shows the expected signature for debugging purposes.

whatIs: The JWT RS256 Verifier verifies that a JSON Web Token signed with the RSA-SHA256 algorithm is authentic by checking the signature against a public key you provide. Unlike HMAC verification (which requires a shared secret), RS256 uses asymmetric cryptography: the token is signed with a private key, and verification uses the corresponding public key. This means the verification key can be safely distributed without compromising token security.
howToUse: Paste the complete JWT into the input panel — all three dot-separated segments.
Paste the RSA public key in the Public Key field — this should be in PEM format (-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----).
Click Verify — the tool extracts the token's signature, reconstructs the signing input, and verifies using the public key.
Read the result — Valid means the signature matches and the token was signed by the corresponding private key.
Check the payload — the decoded payload shows all claims, including expiration, issuer, and subject.
whyUse: RS256 is the standard algorithm for JWT in distributed systems because it separates signing authority (private key) from verification (public key). Services that only need to verify tokens — like API gateways, microservices, and CDNs — can hold just the public key, which is safe to distribute. This tool lets you verify RS256 tokens locally without running a verification server, making it essential for debugging authentication flows in distributed architectures.

faq.q: Where do I get the public key?
faq.a: The public key is generated alongside the private key when you create an RSA key pair. If you're using an identity provider (Auth0, AWS Cognito, Azure AD), the public key is available at the JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) endpoint — usually at /.well-known/jwks.json. Download the key matching the kid (key ID) in the token's header.

faq.q: What format should the public key be in?
faq.a: PEM format is standard: a Base64-encoded key between -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- and -----END PUBLIC KEY----- headers. Most identity providers export keys in this format. The tool also accepts raw Base64 (without headers) for convenience.

faq.q: Can I use this to verify HMAC-signed tokens?
faq.a: No — RS256 and HS256 use fundamentally different cryptographic operations. RS256 uses RSA signature verification; HS256 uses HMAC computation. Use the JWT HS256 Verifier tool for HMAC-signed tokens.

faq.q: What does the kid header field mean?
faq.a: kid (Key ID) identifies which key was used to sign the token. In systems with key rotation (where signing keys change periodically), the kid tells the verifier which public key to use. Check the token's header for the kid, then find the matching key in the JWKS endpoint.

whatIs: The Token Strength Analyzer evaluates the entropy and security of a token or random string by measuring its length, character diversity, and estimated bits of entropy. Paste any token — API key, session token, random string — and the tool reports its length, unique character count, character set composition, and estimated entropy in bits, helping you assess whether the token provides sufficient randomness for its intended purpose.
howToUse: Paste a token, API key, or random string into the input panel.
Read the analysis — the tool shows token length, unique characters, character set composition, and estimated entropy.
Compare the entropy to benchmarks — 80+ bits is strong for API keys, 128+ bits is strong for cryptographic tokens.
Check the character diversity — a token using only lowercase letters has less entropy per character than one using mixed case, digits, and symbols.
whyUse: Not all tokens are created equal. A 12-character token using only lowercase letters has about 56 bits of entropy — crackable with moderate computing power. The same length token using mixed case, digits, and symbols has about 71 bits. Understanding entropy helps you evaluate whether your tokens, API keys, and session identifiers are actually secure or just look random. This tool makes the abstract concept of 'randomness' concrete and measurable.

faq.q: What entropy level is 'secure'?
faq.a: For API keys and session tokens, 80+ bits of entropy is considered secure against brute-force attacks. 128+ bits is the standard for cryptographic operations. For reference, a 16-character password using mixed case, digits, and symbols has about 95 bits of entropy. A 32-character hex string (like an API key) has 128 bits.

faq.q: Why does character diversity matter?
faq.a: Entropy per character depends on the pool of possible characters. A lowercase letter has log2(26) ≈ 4.7 bits of entropy. A character from a 94-character pool (mixed case + digits + symbols) has log2(94) ≈ 6.6 bits. So a 20-character token from a large pool is significantly more secure than the same length from a small pool.

faq.q: Can I use this to generate tokens?
faq.a: This tool analyzes existing tokens. For generation, use the Random API Key Generator or Random Password Generator in the Security category. Those tools use crypto.getRandomValues() for cryptographically secure randomness, while this tool only measures the quality of input you provide.

faq.q: What's the difference between entropy and length?
faq.a: Length is the number of characters; entropy is the amount of information (randomness) in the token. A 100-character token using only the letter 'a' has very low entropy (essentially 0 bits beyond the first character) despite its length. Both length and character diversity contribute to entropy.

whatIs: The Random API Key Generator creates cryptographically secure random API keys using the Web Crypto API's crypto.getRandomValues() function. Generate keys in Hex, Base64, or Base64URL encoding with configurable byte length (8-256 bytes). The output is a single random string suitable for use as API keys, bearer tokens, secret keys, or any context requiring high-entropy random data.
howToUse: Set the byte length — 32 bytes (256 bits) is the default, providing strong security for most use cases.
Choose the encoding format — Hex produces lowercase hex characters (a-f0-9), Base64 uses the standard alphabet (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /), and Base64URL uses the URL-safe alphabet (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, -, _).
Click Generate — the tool produces a single random key using cryptographically secure random number generation.
Copy the key — use it as an API key, bearer token, or secret in your application.
Generate multiple keys if needed — each click produces a new, independent random value.
whyUse: API keys need to be unpredictable and unique — a weak key can be guessed or brute-forced, compromising your entire API. This tool uses the browser's cryptographic random number generator (CSPRNG), which provides the same quality of randomness as operating system entropy sources. The encoding choice matters: Hex is common for AWS and Google Cloud API keys; Base64URL is used by OAuth2 and JWT; standard Base64 is used by many legacy APIs.

faq.q: How many bytes should my API key be?
faq.a: 32 bytes (256 bits) is the standard for most APIs — it provides 2^256 possible values, which is computationally infeasible to brute-force. For high-security applications (financial APIs, healthcare), 48-64 bytes (384-512 bits) provides additional margin. For low-risk internal tools, 16 bytes (128 bits) is sufficient.

faq.q: What encoding should I choose?
faq.a: Check your API's documentation for the expected format. AWS uses Hex; Google Cloud uses Base64; most OAuth2 implementations use Base64URL (which avoids characters that need URL-encoding). If unsure, Hex is the safest default — it's supported everywhere and produces only [0-9a-f] characters.

faq.q: Is this better than using a UUID?
faq.a: For API keys, yes. UUID v4 provides 128 bits of entropy (22 bytes), but its format includes hyphens and is 36 characters long. A 32-byte hex key provides 256 bits of entropy in 64 characters, and its format is more conventional for API keys. UUIDs are better for database identifiers; hex/base64 keys are better for API authentication.

faq.q: Can I use this to generate passwords?
faq.a: Yes, but the Random Password Generator is better for that purpose — it lets you control character sets (uppercase, lowercase, digits, symbols) and produces human-readable output. The API Key Generator is optimized for machine-readable keys in specific encoding formats.

whatIs: The Passphrase Generator creates memorable yet secure passphrases by combining random words from a curated word list with a configurable separator. Generate passphrases with 3-10 words, separated by hyphens, spaces, periods, or custom characters. The output is a phrase like 'correct-horse-battery-staple' that is both easy to remember and computationally strong due to the large word pool.
howToUse: Set the word count — 5 words (default) provides approximately 70 bits of entropy from the word list.
Choose a separator — hyphens (-) are the most common, but you can use spaces, dots, underscores, or any single character.
Click Generate — the tool produces a new passphrase each time.
Copy the passphrase — it's ready to use as a password, encryption key, or recovery phrase.
Regenerate if needed — each click produces a completely independent random phrase.
whyUse: Passphrases solve the fundamental tension between password security and usability. A strong random password like 'k7$Xp2mNq9' is secure but nearly impossible to remember. A passphrase like 'correct-horse-battery-staple' is both memorable and secure — it has 4 words from a 2048-word list, providing approximately 44 bits of entropy (equivalent to a 7-character random password with mixed case, digits, and symbols). The xkcd-style approach of combining random words is now recommended by NIST and security researchers as the preferred method for user-created passwords.

faq.q: How many words should I use?
faq.a: 5 words from the word list provides approximately 70 bits of entropy — sufficient for most applications including password managers and encryption keys. 4 words (56 bits) is adequate for website logins. 6+ words (84+ bits) is appropriate for high-security applications like master passwords or cryptocurrency wallet seeds.

faq.q: What word list does this use?
faq.a: The tool uses a curated list of common English words, selected for memorability and distinctiveness. The list is similar to the EFF diceware word list, which is the standard for passphrase generation. Each word is short, common, and phonetically distinct to minimize confusion.

faq.q: Why not just use a random password?
faq.a: Passphrases are easier to type, remember, and communicate verbally (over the phone or in person). A 20-character random password is more secure but impractical to remember without a password manager. Passphrases provide a good balance: 5 words is about as secure as a 12-character random password, but you can actually remember it.

faq.q: Can I use this for cryptocurrency wallet seeds?
faq.a: Not directly. BIP-39 mnemonic seeds use a specific 2048-word list in a specific order, with a checksum. This generator uses a different word list and doesn't include the BIP-39 checksum. For cryptocurrency wallets, use a BIP-39 compatible tool.

whatIs: The Password Entropy Calculator measures the theoretical randomness of a password by calculating its entropy in bits — the standard unit for measuring cryptographic strength. Enter any password, and the tool determines the character pool size (based on which character types are present), multiplies by the password length, and reports the total entropy. Higher entropy means more resistance to brute-force attacks.
howToUse: Enter a password or random string in the input panel.
Read the entropy calculation — the tool shows the password length, character pool size, and estimated entropy in bits.
Compare against benchmarks — 60 bits is weak, 80 bits is fair, 100+ bits is strong, 128+ bits is excellent.
Understand the breakdown — the character pool tells you which character types contribute to entropy (lowercase: 26, uppercase: 26, digits: 10, symbols: ~32).
whyUse: Entropy is the mathematically rigorous way to measure password strength — not 'how long' or 'how complex' but 'how many possible combinations would an attacker need to try.' A 12-character password using only lowercase letters has 26^12 ≈ 95 bits of entropy. The same length using all character types has 94^12 ≈ 79 bits — actually less, because the pool is larger but the password is the same length. This tool makes these calculations automatic and shows exactly why length matters more than complexity for most passwords.

faq.q: Why is length more important than complexity?
faq.a: Each additional character multiplies the search space by the pool size. A 16-character lowercase password (26^16 ≈ 75 bits) is stronger than an 8-character mixed password (94^8 ≈ 52 bits). Doubling the length squares the search space; adding character types only multiplies by a small factor. NIST now recommends long passwords over complex short ones.

faq.q: What does 'character pool' mean?
faq.a: The character pool is the total number of possible characters a password could contain. Lowercase letters: 26. Uppercase: 26. Digits: 10. Common symbols: ~32. Total mixed: ~94. The pool size determines how much entropy each character position adds. A larger pool means each character is more unpredictable.

faq.q: How does this compare to real-world cracking speed?
faq.a: At 10 billion guesses per second (a modern GPU cluster), a 64-bit entropy password takes about 18 minutes to crack on average. An 80-bit password takes about 38 years. A 128-bit password takes longer than the age of the universe. The tool estimates crack time using the formula: average guesses = 2^entropy / 2.

faq.q: Does this account for dictionary attacks?
faq.a: No — this calculator measures theoretical entropy based on character pool and length. Real-world attacks use dictionary attacks, rule-based mutations, and rainbow tables that can crack common passwords much faster. Use the Password Pattern Analyzer tool to check for dictionary words and common patterns.

whatIs: The Password Pattern Analyzer detects common weak patterns in passwords that reduce their effective entropy below what a simple length/character-pool calculation would suggest. Enter a password, and the tool checks for dictionary words, keyboard patterns (qwerty, asdf), repeated characters (aaa, 111), sequential characters (abc, 123), common substitutions (p@ssw0rd), and other predictable structures that attackers exploit in rule-based cracking.
howToUse: Enter a password in the input panel.
Read the analysis — the tool lists every weak pattern it detects.
Address each flagged issue — the tool suggests specific improvements for each detected pattern.
Re-analyze after changes — paste the improved password to verify the patterns are resolved.
whyUse: Password crackers don't try random combinations — they use dictionaries, rule engines, and pattern databases that exploit human predictability. A password like 'P@ssw0rd123' looks complex (mixed case, symbols, digits) but is trivially crackable because it follows a well-known substitution pattern (P→p, @→a, 0→o, 3→e). This tool identifies these patterns, showing you exactly what an attacker's rule engine would exploit. It's the difference between 'theoretical entropy' (what a calculator shows) and 'practical entropy' (what a cracker actually faces).

faq.q: What patterns does the tool detect?
faq.a: Common patterns include: dictionary words (even with substitutions), keyboard walks (qwerty, zxcvbn), repeated characters (aaa, 111), sequential characters (abc, 123), date patterns (1990, 2024), common passwords (password, letmein), and substitution patterns (p@ssw0rd, h4ck3r).

faq.q: Why is 'P@ssw0rd' weak if it has symbols?
faq.a: Because 'P@ssw0rd' is a known substitution of 'Password' — the @ replaces a, 0 replaces o, etc. Password crackers have rules that try every common word with every common substitution. This specific pattern is one of the first things any cracker tries. The symbols add no entropy because they follow a predictable rule.

faq.q: What makes a password resistant to pattern attacks?
faq.a: Truly random passwords (generated by a password manager or random generator) have no patterns because they're not created by humans. If you must create a memorable password, use 4+ random words (passphrase) rather than a single word with modifications. Randomness is the key — if you can predict any part of the password, a cracker can too.

faq.q: Should I use this with the Password Strength Checker?
faq.a: Yes — use both. The Strength Checker measures theoretical entropy (length × pool). The Pattern Analyzer measures practical entropy (resistance to real-world attacks). A password can score 'strong' on the strength checker but 'weak' on the pattern analyzer if it follows a known pattern.

whatIs: The Common Password Checker compares a password against a built-in list of the most commonly used passwords — the ones that appear in every major data breach and are the first things any password cracker tries. Enter a password, and the tool immediately reports whether it matches a known common password or is safe from this basic check.
howToUse: Enter a password in the input panel.
Read the result — the tool reports whether the password is in the common list or not.
If flagged, replace the password immediately — common passwords are tried first in any attack and are crackable in under a second.
Use this as a first-pass check before using the more detailed Pattern Analyzer or Strength Checker.
whyUse: Before measuring entropy or analyzing patterns, the most basic password check is 'is this password already known to attackers?' The top 100,000 most common passwords (password, 123456, qwerty, etc.) account for a significant percentage of all successful brute-force attacks. This tool catches these instantly. It's the minimum bar for password security — if your password is in this list, no amount of additional complexity matters because attackers try these first.

faq.q: Where does the common password list come from?
faq.a: The list is compiled from publicly available breach data collections (like Have I Been Pwned's password list) and commonly used password dictionaries. It includes the most frequently occurring passwords across billions of real-world breach records.

faq.q: What if my password isn't in the list?
faq.a: Not being in the common list is necessary but not sufficient. A password can be uncommon but still weak (like 'xkcdreference' or 'mydogspot1'). Use the Password Pattern Analyzer for deeper analysis and the Password Strength Checker for entropy measurement.

faq.q: Is this the same as Have I Been Pwned?
faq.a: No — HIBP checks if your email/password has appeared in known breaches. This tool checks if your password is in a common password list. HIBP uses a k-anonymity model (you send a hash prefix, not the actual password); this tool does local checking with no network requests.

faq.q: How often is the list updated?
faq.a: The built-in list is a snapshot of commonly used passwords as of the tool's release. For the most current breach data, use Have I Been Pwned's API or Check Have I Been Pwned. This tool catches the timeless classics that never stop being common.

whatIs: The Password Length Estimator calculates the estimated time required to crack a password of a given length and character pool size using brute-force attacks at various speeds. Configure the password length and character pool, and the tool estimates crack time at 10 billion guesses per second (a modern GPU cluster), helping you understand how length and complexity translate to real-world security.
howToUse: Set the password length — use the slider or input to configure 4-32 characters.
Set the character pool size — 26 for lowercase only, 62 for mixed case + digits, 94 for all printable ASCII.
Read the estimated crack time — the tool shows how long brute-force would take at 10 billion guesses per second.
Adjust parameters to find the sweet spot — the tool helps you balance length against complexity for your security requirements.
whyUse: Understanding crack time makes password policy concrete. Instead of abstract statements like 'use strong passwords,' this tool shows exactly what 'strong' means in terms of time: a 12-character mixed-case password takes about 3 years to crack; a 16-character password takes about 34,000 years. This helps justify password length requirements to stakeholders and helps users understand why 'just one more character' matters enormously.

faq.q: Why 10 billion guesses per second?
faq.a: This represents a realistic attack speed using a modern GPU cluster (like hashcat on 8x RTX 4090 GPUs). Password hashing algorithms like bcrypt at 10 rounds reduce this to about 100,000 guesses per second, making the same password vastly more secure. The 10B/s figure represents the worst case (fast hash algorithms like MD5 or SHA-1).

faq.q: How does password hashing affect crack time?
faq.a: Password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) add a computational cost to each guess. bcrypt with 10 rounds reduces the guessing speed from 10B/s to about 100K/s — a 100,000x slowdown. This means a password that takes 3 years to crack with fast hashing takes 300,000 years with bcrypt. Always use a slow hash algorithm for password storage.

faq.q: What character pool should I assume?
faq.a: Lowercase only: 26. Mixed case: 52. Mixed case + digits: 62. All printable ASCII: 94. For passphrases (4 random words from a 2048-word list): 2048^4 ≈ 44 bits. Choose the pool that matches how the password was actually created, not what it theoretically could contain.

faq.q: Is this accurate for dictionary attacks?
faq.a: No — this estimates pure brute-force time. Dictionary attacks are much faster for common passwords (they can check millions of dictionary words per second). The Password Pattern Analyzer and Common Password Checker handle dictionary-based threats. This tool is for understanding the theoretical strength of random passwords.

whatIs: The PIN Generator creates random numeric PINs of configurable length (3-12 digits) using cryptographically secure random number generation. Each digit is independently generated using crypto.getRandomValues(), ensuring uniform distribution across all possible PIN combinations. The output is a simple numeric string suitable for two-factor authentication, door codes, or temporary access credentials.
howToUse: Set the PIN length — 6 digits (default) is standard for most authentication systems.
Click Generate — the tool produces a random PIN using cryptographic randomness.
Copy the PIN — it's ready to use as a verification code, door code, or temporary credential.
Generate again for a new PIN — each click produces an independent random value.
whyUse: PINs are used everywhere: ATM cards (4 digits), two-factor authentication (6 digits), device pairing (4-8 digits), and temporary access codes (6-8 digits). The security of a PIN depends entirely on its randomness — a PIN generated by a human (like a birthday: 0715) is far weaker than a random one. This tool ensures each digit is uniformly random, making the PIN as strong as its length allows. A random 6-digit PIN has 10^6 = 1,000,000 possible values, requiring an average of 500,000 guesses to crack.

faq.q: How many digits should my PIN be?
faq.a: 6 digits is the standard for most authentication systems — it provides 1 million possible values. 4 digits (10,000 values) is common for convenience (ATM, phone unlock) but weak against systematic guessing. 8 digits (100 million values) is appropriate for high-security applications. The choice depends on the lockout policy — a 4-digit PIN with a 3-attempt lockout is much more secure than a 6-digit PIN with unlimited attempts.

faq.q: Are the digits truly random?
faq.a: Yes — each digit is generated using crypto.getRandomValues(), which is a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG). This is the same quality of randomness used for cryptographic keys and tokens. The digits are uniformly distributed, meaning each of the 10 possible digits (0-9) has exactly a 10% chance for each position.

faq.q: Can I use this for 2FA codes?
faq.a: For TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) codes, the PIN must be generated by a shared secret and the current time — this tool generates random PINs, not time-based ones. For backup codes or recovery PINs, this tool is appropriate. For TOTP, use a dedicated authenticator library.

faq.q: How do I prevent PIN guessing?
faq.a: PINs are inherently low-entropy (6 digits = ~20 bits). The primary defense is lockout after failed attempts (3-5 tries), rate limiting, and account alerts. A 6-digit PIN with a 3-attempt lockout and 15-minute cooldown provides reasonable security for most applications.

whatIs: The Memorable Password Generator creates passwords that are both memorable and secure by combining a random word with random numbers and special characters in a structured format. Each password follows a pattern like Word+Digits+Special+Digits, producing strings like 'Cloud7!29' or 'River4@83' that are easier to remember than fully random strings while maintaining sufficient entropy for most authentication systems.
howToUse: Click Generate to produce a new memorable password.
The tool creates a password following a structured pattern: a common word + digits + special character + more digits.
Copy the password — it's ready to use for accounts where you need to remember the password without a manager.
Generate multiple times to find one you prefer — each output is independently random.
whyUse: Some contexts require passwords that humans can remember without a password manager: shared workstation logins, Wi-Fi passwords, or situations where a password manager isn't available. Fully random passwords like 'k7$Xp2mNq9' are secure but hard to memorize. This generator creates passwords with enough structure to be memorable (a real word) while adding enough randomness (digits, special chars) to resist basic attacks. The tradeoff is lower entropy than a fully random password of the same length, but higher entropy than a human-chosen password.

faq.q: How secure are these passwords?
faq.a: A typical output like 'Cloud7!29' has about 40-50 bits of entropy — adequate for low-risk accounts but not for high-security applications. For maximum security, use the Random Password Generator. For memorability + reasonable security, this tool strikes a practical balance.

faq.q: Why use this instead of a random password?
faq.a: Only when you must remember the password without a password manager. For all other cases, the Random Password Generator produces stronger passwords. This tool is for the specific scenario where memorability is a hard requirement.

faq.q: Can attackers guess these passwords?
faq.a: Rule-based password crackers can attempt common patterns like Word+Number+Symbol+Number. However, the random word selection from a large list and random digit placement make these passwords significantly stronger than human-chosen passwords. They're not as strong as fully random passwords, but they're much stronger than 'password123' or 'MyDogSpot'.

whatIs: The Password Comparison Tool takes two passwords and compares them for exact equality, reporting whether they are identical or different. This is useful for verifying password entries during account creation (confirming the user typed the same password twice), comparing passwords from different sources, or checking whether a stored hash matches an expected value.
howToUse: Enter the first password in the left input panel.
Enter the second password in the right input panel.
Read the result — the tool reports whether the two passwords match exactly.
The comparison is case-sensitive and whitespace-sensitive — 'Password' and 'password' are different.
whyUse: When creating accounts or changing passwords, users typically enter the password twice to catch typos. This tool provides the same comparison without needing a form with two password fields. It's also useful for verifying that a password generator output matches what you intended to save, or for comparing passwords from a password manager export against what you remember.

faq.q: Is this comparison secure?
faq.a: The comparison happens entirely in your browser — passwords are never transmitted or stored. The comparison is a simple string equality check. For timing-safe comparison (preventing timing attacks), use a dedicated cryptographic comparison function in your application code.

faq.q: Does this check password strength?
faq.a: No — this tool only checks whether two inputs are identical. Use the Password Strength Checker or Password Entropy Calculator for strength analysis. This tool is purely for confirming that two entries match.

faq.q: Can I compare hashed passwords?
faq.a: Not directly. If you paste two bcrypt hashes, the tool will report whether the hash strings are identical, but this doesn't verify that the underlying passwords match (different passwords can produce different hashes). For hash comparison, use the Hash Comparison Tool in the Security category.

whatIs: The AES Encryption/Decryption Tool encrypts and decrypts text using the AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) algorithm via the Web Crypto API. Enter plaintext and a password, and the tool derives a 256-bit AES key from the password using PBKDF2 (100,000 iterations), generates a random 12-byte initialization vector (IV), and produces an encrypted string that includes the IV and salt prepended to the ciphertext. Decryption reverses the process using the same password.
howToUse: Select Encrypt or Decrypt mode from the dropdown.
Enter the text to encrypt (or the encrypted string to decrypt) in the input panel.
Enter a password in the Password field — this is used to derive the AES key via PBKDF2.
For encryption: the output is a Base64 string containing salt + IV + ciphertext.
For decryption: paste the encrypted string and enter the same password used for encryption.
whyUse: AES-256-GCM is the gold standard for symmetric encryption — it's used by HTTPS (TLS), VPNs, and disk encryption. GCM mode provides both confidentiality (the data is encrypted) and authenticity (any modification is detected). The PBKDF2 key derivation means the encryption key is derived from a human-readable password, making it practical for encrypting files, messages, or configuration data without managing raw cryptographic keys. All processing happens in the browser — your plaintext never leaves your device.

faq.q: Is this suitable for encrypting sensitive data?
faq.a: For personal use (encrypting notes, files, configuration data before sharing) — yes, this provides strong AES-256-GCM encryption. For production applications, use a well-audited library like the Web Crypto API directly in your application code, with proper key management and storage. This tool is for manual encryption tasks, not as a replacement for application-level encryption.

faq.q: What is PBKDF2 and why does it matter?
faq.a: PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) transforms a human password into a cryptographic key by hashing it 100,000 times with a random salt. This makes brute-force attacks expensive — each password guess requires 100,000 hash computations. Without PBKDF2, an attacker could try billions of passwords per second; with it, they can only try thousands.

faq.q: Can I decrypt data encrypted with this tool using OpenSSL?
faq.a: Not directly. This tool uses a custom format (salt + IV + ciphertext prepended together). OpenSSL uses different formats and headers. For interoperability, use a standard format like PKCS7 or a dedicated file encryption tool. This tool is for encrypting/decrypting within its own ecosystem.

faq.q: What happens if I lose the password?
faq.a: The encrypted data is unrecoverable. AES-256 encryption is computationally infeasible to break without the password. There is no backdoor, no recovery mechanism, and no way to decrypt without the exact password. This is by design — it's what makes the encryption secure. Store your passwords securely.

whatIs: The Rail Fence Cipher Tool encrypts and decrypts text using the Rail Fence (Zigzag) transposition cipher. This classical cipher writes the plaintext in a zigzag pattern across a specified number of 'rails' (rows), then reads off each row to produce the ciphertext. Unlike substitution ciphers (Caesar, Vigenere), the Rail Fence cipher rearranges character positions without changing the characters themselves.
howToUse: Enter the plaintext to encrypt (or ciphertext to decrypt) in the input panel.
Set the number of rails using the options — more rails create a more complex zigzag pattern.
The tool outputs the encrypted (or decrypted) text.
For decryption, use the same number of rails that was used for encryption.
Copy the result using the copy button.
whyUse: The Rail Fence cipher is one of the oldest known encryption methods, used in various forms since ancient times. While trivially breakable by modern standards (there are only N possible rail configurations for N rails), it demonstrates the fundamental concept of transposition ciphers — rearranging data without altering it. Understanding transposition is essential for learning about modern cryptographic principles, and the Rail Fence cipher is the clearest example of this concept. It's also used in CTF challenges, puzzle games, and educational cryptography courses.

faq.q: How does the Rail Fence cipher work?
faq.a: Write the plaintext diagonally in a zigzag pattern across N rails, then read each rail left-to-right. For example, 'HELLO WORLD' with 3 rails: Rail 1: H_L_O__L, Rail 2: _E_O_W_R_D, Rail 3: __L___O. Reading rail by rail gives 'HLOL EOWRD LO'. Decryption reverses this by figuring out how many characters go on each rail.

faq.q: Is this secure?
faq.a: No — it's a classical cipher with only N possible keys (where N is the number of rails). A brute-force attack tries all possible rail counts and picks the one that produces readable text. This tool is for educational purposes, puzzle-solving, and understanding cipher mechanics — not for securing real data.

faq.q: How many rails should I use?
faq.a: More rails create a more complex transposition. 2-3 rails are the classic examples; 5-10 rails create more scrambled output. The maximum meaningful rail count is roughly half the text length (more rails than that just adds empty rows). For educational purposes, 3 rails is the standard starting point.

faq.q: Can I use this for encoding, not encryption?
faq.a: Yes — many people use simple ciphers like Rail Fence for encoding game clues, puzzle challenges, and scavenger hunts. It provides obfuscation without real security, which is perfect for recreational use where you want the recipient to be able to decode it with a hint.
